                            Socioeconomic scenarios

MainAnthropogenic climate change and urbanization are increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events worldwide1,2,3. Billions of people are projected to face severe urban thermal environments within 50 years4. Beyond the known physiological burdens, heat exposure also affects mental health, including suicide risk and subjective well-being5, making compound health-risk assessment a climate priority6,7. Greenhouse gas forcing dominates large-scale warming, while urban heat islands intensify local stress in dense cores8,9,10. Against a greenhouse-gas-warmed baseline, additional urban heat-island warming can push exposure closer to thermal tolerance thresholds11, amplifying health and emotional impacts disproportionately while making urban-form variation central to heat-risk assessment12,13.High-resolution psychological responses to heatwaves remain difficult to measure at scale. Health statistics and retrospective surveys are sparse and delayed, so they often miss short-term discomfort and emotional fluctuations during extreme events14,15. Social media processed with natural language processing can convert expressed sentiment into high-resolution metrics16,17,18. By quantifying sentiment polarity and intensity in unstructured text, social media data provide high-resolution measures of expressed emotion and reveal how responses vary across socioeconomic and infrastructural contexts19,20,21.Despite effectively deconstructing disaster risk into a static superposition of hazard, exposure and vulnerability, traditional resilience frameworks frequently fail to capture the spatiotemporal evolution of urban systems under shock22,23,24. Dynamic resilience theory instead tracks peak intensity, cumulative magnitude and recovery time25,26. Public psychological responses are also shaped by environmental and socioeconomic contexts27. The key uncertainty is whether economic capacity can become an effective emotional buffer under extreme heat28,29,30. Consequently, genuine urban resilience hinges on synergizing the ‘hard capability’ of physical defence with the ‘soft elasticity’ of social recovery.This study develops an event-aligned dual-resilience framework that compares physical heat perturbation with publicly expressed emotional recovery across 357 Chinese cities, identifying where physical heat buffering failed to translate into emotional recovery. By integrating geolocated social sensing data processed through natural-language-processing methods with high-resolution meteorological observations from 2010 to 2024 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2), we calculate two composite metrics: the heat aggregation index (HGI) and the emotional aggregation index (EGI). EGI denotes publicly expressed emotional resilience within heatwave-event windows, not offline mental states themselves. We use a distributed lag nonlinear model (DLNM) to systematically quantify the spatiotemporal asynchrony and lag effects of emotional feedback in response to thermal exposure. Furthermore, we utilize interpretable machine learning methods to identify key determinants of the mismatch, and their threshold effects. Ultimately, we project the co-evolutionary trajectories of physical risk and social adaptation under three distinct pathways: Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. These findings provide a scientific basis for evaluating compound urban heat resilience and offer critical support for formulating precision-guided adaptation strategies.Spatial–temporal characteristics of HGI and EGIAcross 357 Chinese cities, the HGI and EGI exhibited pronounced spatial heterogeneity (Fig. 1a,b). At the national scale, the mean HGI stood at 0.260 (90% confidence interval (CI) 0.256–0.264), while the mean EGI reached 0.444 (90% CI 0.436 to 0.451). Notably, the disparity between the lowest and highest deciles spanned approximately 101.6% for HGI and 96.4% for EGI, a gap that underscores a sharp stratification in urban capacity to physically recover from and emotionally buffer heatwaves. Latitudinal sliding-window profiles revealed a general south-to-north gradient, with cities in Northeast and North China systematically registering higher index values, whereas those in the Yangtze River basin and southern China clustered within low-to-moderate ranges. However, even within narrow 0.8° bands, the 5th–95th percentile envelope remained extensive and often approached a twofold spread. This substantial variability suggested that local attributes, such as urban form, demographic structure and governance, can substantially modulate the resilience baseline established by broad climatic patterns.Fig. 1: Spatial patterns and temporal evolution of HGI and EGI in 357 Chinese cities from 2010 to 2024.Full size imagea,b, National mean values of HGI (a) and EGI (b) from 2010 to 2024 for 357 cities. The main panels show city-level values, with darker colours indicating higher indices. The right-hand panels display latitudinal profiles constructed using a 0.8° sliding window; solid lines indicate the mean within each window and shaded envelopes represent the 5th–95th percentiles of city values. c, Distributions of HGI (red) and EGI (teal) by climatic region and degree of urbanization. Climatic regions comprise tropical–subtropical (TSC), warm temperate (WTC), cold temperate (CTC) and plateau climate (PC), while settlement types comprise megacity cores, small- and medium-sized cities (SME city), other urban areas and rural areas. Centre lines indicate medians, boxes extend from the 25th to the 75th percentiles, whiskers extend to the smallest and largest values within 1.5 times the interquartile range, and values beyond the whiskers are plotted individually as outliers. Black points indicate group means. The lowest and highest plotted observations represent the minima and maxima, respectively. d, Comparison of HGI (orange) and EGI (blue) across the 19 national city clusters: Beibu Gulf (BG), Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei (BTH), Chengdu–Chongqing (CC), Central Guizhou (CGZ), Central Plains (CP), Central Shanxi (CSX), Central Yunnan (CY), Guangdong–Fujian–Zhejiang Coastal (GFZC), Guanzhong Plain (GZP), Huhhot–Baotou–Erdos–Yulin (HBEY), Harbin–Changchun (HC), Lanzhou–Xining (LX), Liaozhongnan (LZN), Middle Yangtze River (MYR), Northern Tianshan (NT), Ningxia–Yellow River (NYR), Pearl River Delta (PRD), Shandong Peninsula (SD) and Yangtze River Delta (YRD). Bars show the mean across cities within each cluster and error bars indicate 90% CIs. e,f, Annual trajectories of HGI (e) and EGI (f) across the 19 city clusters from 2010 to 2024. Solid coloured lines show cluster means, filled circles mark observed annual values and semi-transparent bands indicate 90% CIs obtained by bootstrapping across constituent cities. Basemap data in a and b from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center (https://www.resdc.cn).Stratification by climate region, settlement pattern and city cluster sharpened these spatial contrasts (Fig. 1c,d). Plateau-climate cities showed higher resilience baselines than warm-temperate cities, with mean EGI and HGI higher by 20.8% (90% CI 20.3 to 21.4) and 17.8% (90% CI 17.1 to 18.5), respectively. Along the urban–rural gradient, megacity cores exceeded rural areas by 9.4% for EGI (90% CI 8.7 to 10.1) and 12.2% for HGI (90% CI 11.2 to 13.2), while small and medium-sized cities showed greater volatility, suggesting that emotional resilience did not scale linearly with city size. At the cluster scale, EGI advantages appeared in central inland and north-western basin cities, whereas HGI advantages concentrated in northern and northeastern industrial belts. To expose mechanisms masked by composite indices, HGI was decomposed into heat peak severity (IMAXh), heat recovery time (RTh) and heat cumulative perturbation magnitude (RPh), and EGI into emotion peak severity (IMAXe), emotion recovery time (RTe) and emotion cumulative perturbation magnitude (RPe) (Supplementary Figs. 3–5). Socioeconomic weighting showed the strongest inequality in RTe, whereas composite HGI and EGI were more evenly distributed. This indicates that the main disparity lay in unequal emotional recovery rather than overall resilience levels (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7 and Supplementary Notes 1 and 2).Across 19 urban agglomerations, HGI and EGI decoupled from 2010 to 2024 (Supplementary Fig. 8). HGI fell from 0.728 in 2010 to 0.399 in 2022, a 45.1% decline, and remained 26.2% below 2010 in 2024. EGI declined more mildly, by 19.9% to its 2021 low, then rebounded 8.1% during 2022–2024, remaining 13.4% below 2010. Socioeconomic exposure widened this mismatch: population exposure to physical heat and emotional risk (E_PH and E_PE) rose 28.3% and 29.3%, while gross domestic product (GDP) exposure to physical heat and emotional risk (E_GH and E_GE) rose 36.1% and 51.5% (Supplementary Fig. 9). Together, these results indicate that population burdens increased similarly across both dimensions, whereas GDP exposure grew faster for emotional risk, suggesting that economic growth did not translate into comparable emotional resilience. Log-scale analysis linked the gap to scale-neutral HGI but a ‘prosperity penalty’ in EGI (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Note 3).Identifying regional hotspots of sociophysical mismatchTo identify urban agglomerations requiring differentiated intervention, we compared physical heat intensity and recovery, emotional shock intensity and recovery, and GDP across 357 cities (Fig. 2). The mean-threshold classification showed that economic scale did not eliminate physical vulnerability (Fig. 2a,b). Overall, 52.1% of cities exhibited high-intensity or slow-recovery physical profiles. This share increased to 76.8% in the Middle Yangtze River basin and 71.7% in the Yangtze River Delta. By contrast, about half of the cities in Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei exhibited lower heat intensity and faster recovery, consistent with more favourable geographic and climatic conditions. Emotional vulnerability was more widespread (Fig. 2c,d), with 84.9% of cities experiencing high-intensity emotional shocks. These cities were concentrated in the Yangtze River Delta and along the eastern coast, where emotional sensitivity appeared to exceed physical buffering capacity. Population-weighted results showed a similar pattern (Supplementary Fig. 10).Fig. 2: Interplay of physical heat intensity, social sentiment response and aggregate resilience coupling with economic volume across Chinese cities, through a data-driven pentagonal typology.Full size imagea,c,e, Pentagonal scatter plots mapping 357 cities based on physical heat intensity (a), social sentiment fluctuation (c) and aggregate resilience coupling (e). Unlike conventional plots, the quadrant origin (dashed cross-hairs) is defined by the sample mean (X, Y) of each indicator, representing the average performance. The quadrant with the highest data density is subdivided diagonally to form five distinct typologies (zones 1–5). Circle sizes are scaled by urban GDP. Physical perspective (RTh versus IMAXh; a). Higher values indicate higher vulnerability. Zone 1 represents the most vulnerable ‘high intensity–slow recovery’ type; zone 3 represents the most resilient ‘low intensity–fast recovery’ type; zone 5 denotes the dense intermediate transition type. Social perspective (RTe versus IMAXe; c). Higher values indicate higher sensitivity. Zone 1 signifies ‘high shock–slow recovery’ (high sensitivity); zone 3 signifies ‘low shock–fast recovery’ (emotional stability). Aggregate perspective (HGI versus EGI; e). Higher values indicate stronger resilience (note the axis inversion compared with a and c). Zone 1 indicates ‘double high resilience’ (synergy); zone 3 indicates ‘double vulnerability’ (deficit trap); zone 2 and zone 4 reveal ‘resilience mismatches’, representing physical-leading and emotional-leading adaptation, respectively. b,d,f, Geospatial distribution of the corresponding typologies across 19 major urban agglomerations. Map colours correspond to the zones in the scatter plots (a, c and e, respectively), and dashed coloured lines delineate the boundaries of each urban agglomeration. Basemap data in b,d,f from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center (https://www.resdc.cn).The coupled HGI–EGI assessment revealed a structural mismatch between physical and emotional resilience (Fig. 2e,f). More than 55% of cities in Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei and the Shandong Peninsula were physically resilient but emotionally vulnerable, suggesting that physical buffering did not translate into emotional recovery. The Yangtze River Delta showed the clearest dual vulnerability, with 55.9% of cities exhibiting both weak physical and emotional resilience, consistent with rapid urbanization, intensified urban heat and high social pressure. In the Middle Yangtze River basin, 91.8% of cities exhibited either dual vulnerability or physical vulnerability with comparatively stronger emotional resilience, indicating greater reliance on emotional adaptation where physical capacity remained limited. Bivariate density analysis further showed that HGI and EGI were not linearly coupled and varied jointly with climate and urbanization (Supplementary Figs. 11–13 and Supplementary Note 4).Geographic variation of lagged emotional responses to heatwavesDLNMs selected by Akaike information criterion (AIC) showed that the best lag day (BL) between heat exposure and emotional response increased from the south-eastern coast to the north-western inland and plateau regions (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 1). Coastal urbanized regions had a mean BL of 2.7 days (P < 0.001; 90% CI 2.6 to 2.8), compared with 3.3 days in north-western inland and plateau regions (P < 0.01; 90% CI 3.2 to 3.4). This gradient was robust (Z > 1.96, P < 0.001). At the climate-zone scale, BL rose from 2.6 days in tropical–subtropical to nearly 3.2 days in cold temperate and plateau climate (Fig. 3c). In these colder and higher regions, more cities showed markedly negative Sen slopes (P < 0.05), linking longer lags with more persistent emotional deterioration. Mann–Kendall tests confirmed an overall monotonic trend (P < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 14). Urban areas had shorter mean BL than rural areas (P < 0.05), with mostly positive Sen slopes within the 90% CI, whereas rural slopes remained negative, indicating faster urban recovery but longer negative-emotion accumulation in the countryside (Fig. 3d).Fig. 3: Spatial heterogeneity of the delay between thermal exposure and emotional response across China.Full size imagea, Fifteen-year mean BL between daily maximum temperature and emotion score for all cities in China. Map colours indicate the length of the lag between heatwaves and emotional responses, from short (blue) to long (red); black lines show provincial boundaries and the inset displays island regions. b, Grid-level BL at 0.1° resolution within six representative city clusters, based on regridded emotional fields: YRD, BTH, PRD, CC, LX and HBEY. Warmer colours denote longer BL and thus slower emotional responses, whereas cooler colours indicate shorter BL. c, Superposed-epoch composites of temperature and emotion for four climate zones and for all urban versus rural grids. Panels correspond to TSC, WTC, CTC and PC. d, All urban and rural grids. For each panel, orange bars represent the 25-day evolution of the average daily maximum temperature, and blue lines represent the corresponding average emotion score. Temperature series are calculated from daily maximum temperature, whereas emotion scores are originally derived from 3-hourly data and then averaged to daily values for visualization. e, Event-averaged temperature and sentiment trajectories for six representative cities (Shanghai, Guangzhou, Beijing, Chongqing, Lanzhou and Eerduosi) across the 25-day W_seq window, generated via superposed epoch analysis. The sentiment data, originally processed at 3-h resolution, were aggregated to daily means here for visual coregistration with daily maximum temperature. These daily composites are presented as trend illustrations of the temperature-emotion coupling; quantitative lag estimates are derived from 3-h resolution DLNM cross-basis fits and reported in Supplementary Table 1. Basemap data in a and b from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center (https://www.resdc.cn).To complement the city-level BL parameters from 3-h DLNM analysis (Supplementary Table 1), we generated event-averaged daily temperature-emotion composites for six representative cities at 0.1° resolution (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16). Shanghai and Guangzhou showed modest, short-lived emotional declines that returned to baseline after temperatures fell. Lanzhou showed delayed drops several days after the heat peak, with BL values near 3.3 days (P < 0.01), while Beijing and Chongqing also showed prolonged lags. These patterns suggested that climate setting and development pathway jointly shaped the timing of emotional responses, with stronger asymmetric vulnerability in northern inland and plateau regions (Supplementary Note 5).Nonlinear determinants of HGI and EGITo capture nonlinear drivers of HGI, EGI and BL, we used an interpretable LightGBM–SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework (Fig. 4, Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Notes 6–8). For HGI, socioeconomic and land-cover factors contributed 37.4% and 32.0% of feature importance, exceeding urban form and geo-environmental factors, each around 15%. GDP was the leading predictor (27.9%), followed by digital elevation model (DEM) (16.1%) and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) (14.7%). Its effect weakened from +0.003 in the lower 50% of the GDP distribution (90% CI −0.009 to 0.011) to almost zero in the upper 25%, indicating diminishing returns to economic capacity. NDVI showed a similar pattern, declining from +0.007 (90% CI −0.013 to 0.014) in the lower half to +0.002 (90% CI 0.001 to 0.005) in the upper 25%, suggesting that greening benefits were strongest in vegetation-poor cities.Fig. 4: The effect of each feature on HGI and EGI.Full size imagea,d, Global importance and local effect of each feature in the ensemble learning models for HGI (a) and EGI (d). In these panels, the x axis shows the SHAP value and the y axis lists the features; point colour ranges from blue to red to indicate low to high feature values. b,e, The global importance of each feature for HGI (b) and EGI (e), expressed as its mean absolute SHAP value divided by the sum over all features. c, SHAP dependence plots for GDP, DEM, NDVI and BD on HGI. f, SHAP dependence plots for GDP, IMAXh, RPh and RTh on EGI. In c and f, the x axis shows the observed feature value and the y axis shows the corresponding SHAP value, representing the local effect on HGI or EGI. Orange curves represent spline-fitted conditional mean SHAP values, and shaded bands indicate the corresponding 90% prediction intervals. Grey histograms show the marginal distributions of feature values, while darker point clouds indicate higher sample density.The EGI model further incorporated IMAXh, RPh and RTh (Fig. 4d–f). These heat-hazard variables accounted for 39.3% of total feature importance, exceeding socioeconomic factors (18.7%) and matching the combined contribution of land cover and urban form. EGI increased almost monotonically with IMAXh, with a one-standard-deviation increase in the upper quartile raising EGI by 0.021 (90% CI 0.017 to 0.025), compared with 0.006 for GDP (90% CI 0.004 to 0.008). RPh and RTh had the strongest effects near their medians, increasing EGI by 0.012 (90% CI 0.011 to 0.015) and 0.006 (90% CI 0.004 to 0.009), respectively. Thus, EGI was driven more by event intensity, cumulative burden and recovery rhythm than by long-term structural capacity. BL attribution further showed that physical heat intensity tended to prolong emotional response, whereas economic capacity compressed it (Supplementary Note 8 and Supplementary Fig. 17).Future projections of heat resilience and exposureConsidering that Chinese cities were expected to face increasingly complex heatwave risk patterns, we used the multimodel ensemble (MME) mean of 13 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models to project changes in EGI and HGI under the SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios (Fig. 5a,b and Extended Data Fig. 6). Over 2025–2050, national mean EGI and HGI across the three scenarios decreased by 6.3% (90% CI 1.4% to 10.9%) and 5.0% (90% CI 3.3% to 8.3%) respectively, indicating that emotional resilience eroded systematically faster than physical defences even in the near term. In relative terms, EGI declined approximately 26% faster than HGI over this near-term horizon, establishing an early-onset divergence that widened the physical–emotional vulnerability gap towards the 2100s. From 2050 to 2100, under SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5, national mean EGI decreased by 5.9% (90% CI −18.2% to +4.4%) and 18.2% (90% CI −26.4% to −10.0%), respectively, relative to 2025; under SSP5-8.5, EGI exhibited a precipitous decline to 0.55 by 2100 (90% CI 0.49 to 0.57), a 22.4% reduction (90% CI 20.1% to 31.5%). Over the same period, HGI decreased in all three scenarios, with the SSP5-8.5 national mean dropping to 0.29 (90% CI 0.27 to 0.33), a 28.5% reduction (90% CI 20.4% to 34.0%). Spatially, during 2025–2050, eastern coastal and central high-density urban agglomerations were the first to show concurrent declines in EGI and HGI (Supplementary Figs. 18 and 19).Fig. 5: Future changes in heatwave resilience and socioeconomic exposure under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.Full size imagea,b, Spatial patterns of the MME mean heatwave resilience index (HGI; a) and emotional resilience index (EGI; b) across China, averaged over 2025–2100 under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. Colours indicate index values in each grid cell, ranging from low (light) to high (dark), with warm colours for HGI and blue–green colours for EGI. c–f, National trajectories of GDP exposure to physical heat risk (E_GH; c), population exposure to physical heat risk (E_PH; d), GDP exposure to emotional risk (E_GE; e) and population exposure to emotional risk (E_PE; f) from 1980 to 2100. Black lines represent annual MME means for the historical period (1980–2014), while blue, green and red lines represent annual MME means under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, respectively. Shaded bands indicate the corresponding intermodel 5th–95th percentile ranges across 13 CMIP6 models. Basemap data in a and b from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center (https://www.resdc.cn). Emo, emotional response.Under SSP5-8.5, these regions evolved into critical risk zones characterized by the simultaneous collapse of emotional and physical resilience during 2050–2100 (Supplementary Fig. 20). Critically, unlike the localized resilience observed in lower-emission scenarios, western and plateau urban agglomerations also experienced substantial erosion in EGI alongside persistently low HGI. This shift indicated a transition from an imbalanced resilience pattern to a systemic vulnerability trap, where the historical psychological buffer was rapidly depleted under compound extreme events. Decomposing the attenuation of HGI and EGI into component drivers revealed that, under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, recovery lags for heat and emotion (RTh and RTe) surged by 33.5–42.7% (90% CI 13.2% to 64.5%), outpacing the 24.4–35.6% rise in peak intensity (IMAXh and IMAXe; 90% CI 5.5% to 53.4%), while cumulative loads (RPh and RPe) rose in parallel by 33.4–36.2% (90% CI 13.1% to 57.0%). This disparity indicated that the core mechanism of resilience failure lay not in the elevation of shock peaks, but in the structural paralysis of system recovery mechanisms (Extended Data Figs. 7–9 and Supplementary Note 9).Population exposure (E_PH and E_PE), GDP exposure (E_GH and E_GE) and the heat-risk exposure ratio (R_HE) further showed that socioeconomic burden intensified faster than physical risk alone (Fig. 5c–f and Extended Data Fig. 10). From 2025 to 2100, GDP exposure to physical heat increased by 59.2% (90% CI 6.0% to 133.9%), 119.3% (90% CI 80.5% to 164.7%) and 144.0% (90% CI 87.4% to 248.0%) under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, while GDP exposure to emotional risk rose by 151.8% (90% CI 131.5% to 210.1%), 145.8% (90% CI 103.2% to 182.9%) and 224.3% (90% CI 155.9% to 284.2%). Under SSP5-8.5, E_GH increased from 3.0 × 103 (90% CI 2.0 × 103 to 3.8 × 103) to 7.2 × 103 (90% CI 5.5 × 103 to 1.0 × 104), whereas E_GE rose from 2.5 × 103 (90% CI 2.3 × 103 to 3.3 × 103) to 8.1 × 103 (90% CI 6.4 × 103 to 9.6 × 103). Population exposure to physical heat increased by 31.2%, 59.8% and 122.2%, and population exposure to emotional risk by 23.9%, 51.0% and 86.2% across the three scenarios. The heat-risk exposure ratio rose by 19.0% (90% CI 11.4% to 25.8%) during 2025–2050 and 32.3% (90% CI 22.6% to 45.7%) during 2050–2100, reaching 1.27 (90% CI 1.16 to 1.45), 1.17 (90% CI 0.89 to 1.35) and 1.46 (90% CI 1.28 to 1.68) by 2100. These results indicated that emotional exposure grew faster than physical heat exposure, especially in eastern and central urban agglomerations under strong forcing.DiscussionPrevailing research often conceptualized urban climate adaptation as a linear progression from physical exposure to social response, a simplification that overlooked the structural mismatch between objective environmental limits and subjective public perception. To address this gap, we utilize multisource data across 357 Chinese cities to establish a comprehensive framework evaluating both physical (HGI) and emotional (EGI) resilience indices. Rather than separately mapping heat exposure or public sentiment, this study identify recovery failure as a measurable cross-domain mechanism through which physical buffering, emotional recovery and socioeconomic exposure become progressively decoupled. We find that emotional recovery is not synchronized with physical mitigation but instead shaped by regional development levels and cognitive differences. Future projections also warn that economic growth or spontaneous adaptation alone could not reverse the continued rise in high-risk exposure. The results indicate that governance needs to move from reactive coping to proactive planning, positioning psychosocial adaptive capacity at the core to minimize the silent accumulation of vulnerability.The divergence between physical and emotional resilience reflects not only meteorological intensity but also perception and governance. Sustained nighttime heat and post-peak recovery shaped discomfort accumulation and delayed emotional restoration despite infrastructural mitigation15,31. EGI should therefore be interpreted as a publicly expressed emotional response mediated by socioeconomic conditions, infrastructure availability, behavioural exposure and risk communication, rather than as a direct individual-level effect of outdoor temperature on mental state32. Apparent adaptation often reflected short-term coping rather than removal of physiological constraints, leaving emotional fluctuations persistent across heterogeneous populations33,34. Social cognitive mechanisms also amplified the gap between objective protection and subjective safety, particularly in developed cities where heuristic biases and risk literacy disparities heightened sensitivity35. Development may therefore create a prosperity penalty, as digital environments and rising safety expectations diffuse anxiety and weaken the stabilizing effect of physical infrastructure36. This pattern aligns with Wilkinson’s inequality–anxiety framework37, in which dense and unequal contexts raise baseline psychological burden through chronic status anxiety and reduce the capacity to absorb additional climate stressors38.A key contribution of this study was to quantify the lag between physical heat and emotional resilience. Emotional stress did not coincide with heat peaks but emerged after a delay. Developed coastal cities showed short elastic fluctuations, whereas north-western inland and plateau regions showed systemic response delays, probably because limited infrastructure slowed artificial heat relief and left recovery more dependent on natural cooling39. Information diffusion may also sustain public attention for days after extreme events, extending emotional impacts21,40. Consequently, early warning systems must shift from focusing solely on meteorological peaks to extending psychological support into the post-heatwave recovery phase18. Particularly in plateau, inland and rural hinterlands, extending psychological support into the post-peak recovery phase yields greater efficacy than confining interventions to the acute hazard onset41,42. Operationally, the HGI–EGI mismatch can guide differentiated heat-action planning. Cities with high HGI but delayed EGI require recovery-side measures, including post-heatwave mental-health outreach, community support networks and nighttime cooling spaces near dense residential and commuting areas. Cities with low HGI and low EGI require combined physical and social measures, such as cooling-centre access, shaded walking routes, ventilation corridors, power-grid stress testing and targeted checks on older adults, outdoor workers and low-income residents. Because emotional responses lagged heat peaks by about 2.7–3.3 days, heat plans should extend risk communication and support into the post-peak recovery period.Mechanistic analysis showed that HGI and EGI followed distinct pathways. HGI exhibited adaptive saturation, as the protective effects of capital accumulation and ecological improvement diminished after reaching a threshold43. This limits the value of incremental infrastructure upgrades alone. EGI was more sensitive to event characteristics, indicating that governance should shift from static resource accumulation to dynamic crisis management6,44. Underdeveloped cities may still benefit from economic and ecological investment45, whereas developed cities need stronger soft adaptation capacity, including risk communication and recalibrated safety expectations46,47. Development can therefore improve physical protection while dense activity, faster urban rhythms and rising expectations compress the emotional repair window, producing a prosperity penalty and accelerated social metabolism (Supplementary Notes 2, 3 and 8). This pattern extends Scitovsky’s joyless economy hypothesis to urban climate adaptation, where comfort infrastructure saturates physical resilience without proportional gains in EGI48.Scenario projections indicated that urban heat risk increasingly reflects exposure lock-in, not only background warming. Under SSP5-8.5, population-based exposure increased by 86.2–122.2% and GDP-based exposure by 144.0–224.3% by 2100, showing how location advantages and investment returns can steer growth into high-risk zones49,50,51. Delayed risk recognition may further allow hazards to accumulate until future extremes exceed historical design levels, triggering surging electricity and cooling demand and cascading infrastructure failures52,53. Governance should therefore move upstream from response to planning, embedding heat risk into investment decisions, power-grid stress tests and cooling provision54,55. These findings empirically ground recent Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) warnings56. Recovery-end degradation under SSP5-8.5, especially the sensitivity of emotional recovery time, suggested that many Chinese cities may approach soft limits of emotional adaptation before comparable HGI transitions emerge. The faster decline of EGI also indicated growing non-economic loss and damage, an AR6 dimension still underquantified in current assessments (Supplementary Note 10). This burden is consistent with Evans’ cumulative environmental stressors framework, in which coexisting urban stressors amplify mental-health costs in dense metropolitan cores57.MethodsDataCity selectionThe initial sample included 372 city-level units with geolocated Weibo records during 2010–2024. Because HGI and EGI required identifiable heatwave events and event-window sentiment trajectories, we excluded cities without valid heatwaves, without valid Weibo observations during heatwave windows or with posting volumes below the 98% confidence criterion. This screening retained 357 cities for HGI–EGI coupling analysis.Emotion dataOur Sina Weibo streaming application programming interface query returned approximately 55 million geotagged posts for 2010–2024. These posts were processed in four steps: relevance prescreening with a 260-term lexicon selected from the DLUT Chinese Sentiment Vocabulary Ontology (27,000+ entries) across five subjective-experience dimensions, retaining 42 million posts; sentiment quantification with HFL-Chinese-BERT-WWM; spatiotemporal matching to 10,863 heatwave-event windows, yielding 22 million event-window posts for EGI calculation; and city-level plus 0.1° grid-level aggregation. The lexicon removed advertisements, news reposts, pure links and other content unrelated to subjective experience rather than identifying heat-related posts. The heatwave–emotion linkage was defined by spatiotemporal co-occurrence, and each retained record preserved text, coordinates and timestamps58.Historical meteorological dataTo characterize the long-term meteorological context, we used the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset to retrieve hourly climate variables at a 0.1° spatial resolution. Meteorological series were extracted by identifying the grid cell nearest to the centroid of each target mesh, after which we computed the daily maximum (Tmax), minimum (Tmin) and mean temperatures for each unit across the 1980–2024 study period. Finally, city-specific thermal profiles were synthesized by calculating the spatially weighted average of all grid cells encompassed within the respective urban boundaries.Future meteorological dataProjected daily Tmax and Tmin were derived from CMIP6 global climate model (GCM) simulations. Historical runs included all-forcing (ALL), greenhouse-gas (GHG) and natural-forcing (NAT) experiments1,7. We retained 13 GCMs with at least three members per forcing experiment (Supplementary Table 3) and assessed SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, representing stringent mitigation, intermediate mitigation and high emissions50,51.For each GCM and SSP, bias-corrected temperature fields drove the full uncertainty propagation pipeline with 1,000 bootstrap samples and 100 LightGBM replicates. The 13-GCM MME mean was reported in Fig. 5 and Extended Data Fig. 10, while the 5th–95th percentiles across all GCM × bootstrap × Monte Carlo replicates defined the 90% confidence band, capturing intermodel spread, EGI uncertainty and model-training variability.Population and GDP dataPopulation projections for China were obtained from the Spatial Population Scenarios database as 1 km × 1 km grids for 2010–2100 under three SSPs, covering the 2010–2024 historical and 2025–2100 future periods. City-level population was summed within urban boundaries. Historical and projected gridded GDP data from WorldPop were harmonized to the same SSPs and aggregated to municipalities for socioeconomic exposure assessment.Auxiliary datasetsAuxiliary variables included Global Urban Boundaries (GUB) urban boundaries, 1-km Köppen–Geiger climate zones, elevation and slope from the Resource and Environment Science and Data Center, 30 m China Land Cover Dataset (CLCD) land cover, 1 km MOD13A3 NDVI and Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) built-environment metrics. The 2018 GUB data delineated urban and rural areas, while building density (BD), building height (BH) and floor area ratio (FAR) were calculated from GHSL grids and aggregated to cities by weighted averaging (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Note 6).Statistical analysisDefinitions of heatwavesIdentification of heatwave events relies on the synthesized Tmax series, utilizing an adaptive compound threshold framework. Relative to the 1980–2014 baseline, we established a dual-criterion system: an absolute threshold (Tabs) fixed at 35 °C, reflecting human physiological tolerance and China Meteorological Administration standards, and a relative threshold (Trel) defined as the 95th percentile within a 15-day moving window to filter seasonal background noise. Addressing China’s climatic heterogeneity, the determination logic remains spatially adaptive. For most urban areas, heatwave days are classified by the simultaneous satisfaction of both criteria (\({T}_{\max }\ge {T}_{\rm{abs}}\cap {T}_{\max } > {T}_{\rm{rel}}\)). By contrast, for high-latitude or cold-region cities where summer extremes seldom reach 35 °C, the protocol applies only the relative threshold, ensuring the capture of statistically warming anomalies specific to those local climates.A discrete heatwave event was defined by the persistence of daily maximum temperatures meeting the aforementioned criteria for at least three consecutive days1. Within the 2010–2024 study period, the protocol permitted the identification of multiple non-overlapping events within a single city for any given year. Each event i was anchored by its onset date \({D}_{\rm{start}}(i)\), which formed the basis for a standardized sliding window of 25 days, denoted as \({W}_{\text{seq}}(i)=\left[{D}_{\text{start}}(i)-10,{D}_{\text{start}}(i)+14\right]\). This temporal sequence explicitly incorporated a 10-day precursor phase, designed to capture the synoptic-scale accumulation of atmospheric circulation processes before the thermal outbreak. Ultimately, the systematic extraction of corresponding spatiotemporal raster series established a standardized database of 10,863 independent samples, serving as the empirical foundation for quantifying the underlying physical mechanisms and social impacts (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2). Because sentiment extraction was driven by identified heatwave-event windows rather than by calendar time, non-heatwave periods, including the 2020 winter–spring COVID lockdown period, were not used to calculate EGI.Processing of sentiment time seriesTo assess public psychological responses during heatwaves, 22 million geotagged Weibo comments were spatially and temporally aligned with the standardized heatwave event windows (Wseq). These data were used as social-sensing records of collective emotional expression, rather than as replacements for individual heat-exposure measurements, population-representative surveys or clinical mental-health assessments59. EGI therefore represents an expression-layer measure rather than a direct measure of latent psychological reality. Because Weibo posts may be shaped by self-presentation, selective expression, event attention and interactive diffusion, EGI captures the collective trajectory of publicly expressed emotions during heatwave windows, not individual offline mental states or clinical mental-health burdens. The use of social media-derived emotional signals to construct EGI was grounded in Situational Crisis Communication Theory, which treats public emotion as an observable response to risk communication, crisis preparation and recovery60. EGI extends this logic from discrete emotion ratios to a continuous event-resolved trajectory decomposed into peak severity, recovery time and cumulative emotional load. Sentiment was quantified using HFL-Chinese-BERT-WWM, a whole-word-masking model optimized for Chinese semantic representation and stronger than the original Google bert-base-chinese on Chinese natural-language-processing benchmarks. All posts passing stage 1 entered BERT inference unconditionally, with no content-based branching61. Following fine-tuning, the model generated probability distributions for positive (Ppos), neutral (Pneu) and negative (Pneg) categories for each comment. On this basis, we defined a continuous sentiment score S(p) on the interval [−1, 1], calculated as S(p) = Ppos − Pneg. This formulation effectively transformed unstructured textual data into high-fidelity emotional valence metrics, enabling precise quantification of public sentiment dynamics (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2).The construction of city-level daily sentiment time series served to characterize the collective emotional fluctuations throughout heatwave episodes. For each day t encompassed by the standardized window Wseq, the analysis aggregated the full ensemble of comments geolocated within the urban perimeter. This spatial integration allowed the computation of the city-wide daily mean sentiment score:$${S}_{\rm{city}}\left(c,t\right)=\frac{1}{\left|P\left(c,t\right)\right|}\sum _{p\in P\left(c,t\right)}S\left(\,p\right)$$
                    (1)
                At 0.1° resolution, geolocated posts were aggregated into grid-level daily sentiment means and interpolated with Ordinary Kriging to convert sparse point observations into continuous intra-urban emotional surfaces. The semivariogram-based interpolation modelled spatial autocorrelation and provided best linear unbiased estimates for unsampled cells. Daily surfaces were then stacked into 25-day sentiment raster sequences for each heatwave event, aligned with physical heat exposure at the pixel scale.Definitions of HGI and EGIResilience is conceptually defined as the capacity of a system to minimize functional degradation and accelerate recovery following anomalous perturbations62. Because urban thermal and social-media sentiment series are non-stationary, static baselines may conflate long-term trends with short-term heatwave perturbations63. We therefore used fast Fourier transform to separate routine equilibrium dynamics from anomalies. Inverse transformation reconstructed a dynamic baseline (Xtrend), and subtracting this baseline yielded zero-mean residuals. Three primitives were extracted from each residual trajectory: peak severity (IMAXt), measuring maximum deviation; recovery time (RTt), measuring the time required to return from the peak to dynamic equilibrium; and cumulative perturbation magnitude (RPt), measuring the area under the anomaly curve. These primitives correspond to Bruneau’s resilience-triangle theory and the resistance-recovery framework widely used in infrastructure, community and social-media-based lifeline resilience studies64. HGI and EGI extend this lineage by applying the same decomposition to physical thermal and emotional disturbance responses within a unified form.To assess systemic resilience, we constructed HGI and EGI from the three primitives, IMAXt, RTt and RPt, for physical thermal and emotional trajectories, respectively. Because simple linear weighting cannot capture constraints among resilience components, we used a hybrid compensatory and non-compensatory model. Max-normalization inversion converted all cost-type indicators into benefit-type scores on [0, 1], where higher values indicate stronger resilience and all components are comparable before aggregation. The composite index is given by$${\rm{Agg}}_{\rm{index}}^{\rm{t}}=\alpha \mathop{\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{{\rm{RT}}_{\rm{t}}}{{\rm{RT}}_{{\rm{t}},\max }}\right)}}\limits_{\rm{Rapidity}\,}+(1-\alpha )\mathop{\underbrace{\left[\left(1-\frac{{\rm{IMAX}}_{\rm{t}}}{{\rm{IMAX}}_{{\rm{t}},\max }}\right)\times \left(1-\frac{{\rm{RP}}_{\rm{t}}}{{\rm{RP}}_{{\rm{t}},\max }}\right)\right]}}\limits_{\mathrm{Resistance}\,}$$
                    (2)
                The aggregation form follows a non-compensatory logic: RT enters linearly because partial recovery still provides proportional benefit, whereas IMAX and RP are coupled multiplicatively to avoid classifying cities with rapid recovery but extreme peak shocks or cumulative loads as highly resilient25. α was retained as a symbolic weight to keep the framework extensible. Perturbation tests over α ∈ {1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2} showed that α = 1/3 produced the highest Spearman rank consistency with alternative weights (mean ρ = 0.948 for HGI and 0.977 for EGI; Supplementary Fig. 21), indicating stable cross-city rankings. Thus, the linear term captured rapidity, while the multiplicative term represented resistance and absorptive capacity. EGI was not derived from raw posting volume or a single-day sentiment mean, but from standardized heatwave-event trajectories through IMAXe, RTe and RPe, capturing the relative intensity, persistence and recovery capacity of collective emotional expression65.AIC-optimized DLNM construction and temporal feature extractionTo estimate delayed and nonlinear effects of heatwaves on expressed sentiment, we used a DLNM with a cross-basis function that jointly modelled the temperature–sentiment association and lag structure66. To avoid bias from fixed lag choices, candidate maximum lags of 0–7 days were fitted for each spatial unit, and the model with the lowest AIC was selected. Heat exposure was represented by quadratic splines and lag days by natural splines, allowing nonlinear thermal effects and delayed emotional responses to be estimated jointly. The AIC-selected lag window was then used to extract IMAXe, RTe and RPe from the reduced lag-response curve. Although IMAXe and RPe were derived from the same fitted response curve, IMAXe measured peak intensity, whereas RPe measured cumulative load as the area under the curve67. The core equation and cross-basis function were defined as follows:$${Y}_{t}=\alpha +s({x}_{t},{\rm{lag}};\eta )+\gamma {{\boldsymbol{Z}}}_{t}+{\varepsilon }_{t}$$
                    (3)
                $$s({x}_{t},{\mathrm{lag}};\eta )=\mathop{\sum}\limits_{j=1}^{{v}_{x}}\mathop{\sum}\limits_{k=1}^{{v}_{l}}{\eta }_{jk}({\phi }_{j}({x}_{t})\times {\psi }_{k}({\mathrm{lag}}))$$
                    (4)
                where \({Y}_{t}\) denotes the sentiment score at time t, \(\alpha\) represents the model intercept, and s(xt, lag; η) serves as the cross-basis function. This function was constituted by a bilinear combination of basis functions for two dimensions: the heat exposure dimension, ϕj(xt), modelled via quadratic splines; and the lag dimension, ψk(lag), modelled via natural splines. Furthermore, Zt signifies the vector of control covariates, \(\gamma\) denotes the corresponding coefficient vector, and εt accounts for the model residuals. Through an AIC minimization screening process, the optimal lag period parameter (BL) was definitively identified for each spatial unit.After the optimal lag structure and BL were identified, a slicing and reduction step was used to quantify heatwave impact characteristics. This procedure reduced the three-dimensional exposure-lag-response surface to a one-dimensional lag-response curve by fixing heat exposure at the city-specific extreme-temperature threshold (xt = Text), thereby extracting a conditional response function with respect to lag days from the cross-basis matrix. The mathematical formulation for the sliced effect curve is expressed as$$\beta (l| {T}_{\rm{ext}})=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{k=1}^{{v}_{l}}\eta k\cdot \psi kl$$
                    (5)
                where β(l|Text) denotes the marginal deviation of public sentiment scores relative to the baseline state on day l following the onset of an extreme heat event. Furthermore, ψk(l) corresponds to the natural spline basis functions along the lag dimension, while \({\tilde{\eta }}_{k}\) signifies the linear coefficient vector, recombined subsequent to fixing the temperature dimension. Predicated on this derived one-dimensional response curve, the three aforementioned core resilience metrics were formally defined as functions of the curve’s morphological characteristics:$${\rm{IMAX}}_{\rm{t}}={\max }_{l\in \left[0,{\rm{BL}}\right]}\left|\beta \left({l|}{T}_{\text{ext}}\right)\right|$$

                    (7)
                $${\mathrm{RP}}_{{\rm{t}}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{l=0}^{\mathrm{BL}}\,\beta \left({l|}{T}_{\text{ext}}\right).$$

                Empirical modellingWe used an interpretable LightGBM–SHAP framework to identify nonlinear drivers of HGI, EGI and BL. To reduce sensitivity to data noise and parameter uncertainty, Monte Carlo simulation was performed through 100 independent stochastic trials, with Bayesian Optimization used in each trial to select hyperparameters68. SHAP then quantified the marginal contribution of urban variables to resilience across the ensemble models. Cross-validation across 19 urban agglomerations confirmed the robustness of the attribution results (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Note 7). Temporal extrapolation was further tested by training LightGBM on 2010–2022 data and blindly predicting 2023–2024 outcomes. All 19 city clusters achieved validation R2 > 0.75, supporting the use of the trained model for SSP-based future projections (Supplementary Note 7). Future integration of explicit LCZ classifications with the HGI–EGI framework could further clarify morphology-specific contributions to physical–emotional resilience divergence.Extreme heat exposure indexesThese metrics were derived exposure-burden indicators rather than independent resilience indices, linking HGI and EGI to demographic and economic carriers exposed to heat risk. We established a coupled physical–social exposure framework anchored in population (POP) and economic (GDP) carriers. Physical heat exposure indices, E_GH and E_PH, measured the socioeconomic load per unit of HGI. Because HGI was defined as a benefit-type resilience indicator, population or GDP was divided by HGI to quantify demographic or economic pressure per unit of physical heat resilience. The exposure metric was calculated as follows:$${\rm{E}}_{-}{\rm{PH}}=\frac{\rm{POP}}{{\rm{HGI}}+\epsilon },{\rm{E}}_{-}{\rm{GH}}=\frac{\rm{GDP}}{{\rm{HGI}}+\epsilon }$$
                    (9)
                Correspondingly, the emotional vulnerability exposure indices (E_GE and E_PE) utilized EGI to quantify the socioeconomic burden sustained per unit of emotional carrying capacity. This formulation allowed emotional exposure to be expressed on the same carrier basis as physical heat exposure, while preserving the interpretation of EGI as socially expressed emotional resilience. The computation was governed by the following formula:$${\rm{E}}_{-}{\rm{PE}}=\frac{\rm{POP}}{{\rm{EGI}}+\epsilon },{\rm{E}}_{-}{\rm{GE}}=\frac{\rm{GDP}}{{\rm{EGI}}+\epsilon }$$
                    (10)
                Finally, to discern the asynchrony between physical environmental conditions and public responses, the physical–emotional bias ratio (R_HE) was constructed. R_HE was therefore interpreted as a relative bias ratio between physical heat exposure and socially expressed emotional exposure, rather than as a standalone resilience index. This metric facilitated a direct juxtaposition of physical safety standards against socially perceived resilience:$${\rm{R}}_{-}{\rm{HE}}=\frac{\rm{HGI}}{{\rm{EGI}}+\epsilon }$$
                    (11)
                Spatiotemporal equity and local heterogeneity analysisA multiscale equity assessment framework encompassing both macro and micro dimensions was established. At the macro level, Gini Coefficients for HGI, EGI and their sub-indicators were computed, weighted specifically by POP, GDP and geographic area (Area), alongside the construction of Lorenz curves. Quantification of the curve’s deviation from the line of equality characterized the concentration effects of resource allocation or risk burdens within specific demographic groups and spatial domains. Conversely, at the micro scale, to capture localized spatial polarization, the local disparity index was introduced. By calculating the absolute deviation between each grid unit and the mean of its topological neighbours, this metric identified distinct ‘inequality highlands’ or ‘depressions’ that were notably decoupled from their surrounding environments.Sensitivity and robustness analysesFor the assessment of GCM, the study selected a suite of 13 models from the CMIP6 (Supplementary Table 3). Using the ECMWF ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset as the observational benchmark, a Taylor diagram facilitated a multidimensional performance assessment of each model. Model performance was summarized with a Taylor diagram using correlation coefficient, centred root-mean-square difference and standard deviation, and differences were tested with a non-parametric Wilcoxon test (Extended Data Fig. 4). The equidistant cumulative distribution function method was then used to bias-correct raw temperature fields, which were downscaled to 0.1° resolution by bilinear interpolation. This MME approach reduced systematic biases from individual GCMs and improved the robustness of future extreme-heat exposure projections.Temporal-granularity sensitivity was tested with the Mann–Kendall trend test across alternative resolutions for all cities (Supplementary Fig. 12 and Supplementary Table 1). The 3-h series showed the most pronounced pattern, with P values consistently below 0.05, so this resolution was used for subsequent resilience-index calculations (Supplementary Notes 5). To reduce interpretability bias from feature redundancy, variance inflation factor (VIF) and Pearson correlation diagnostics were applied, excluding variables with VIF >5 or |r| > 0.8 (Supplementary Fig. 22). We also correlated city-level EGI with heatwave-related Weibo post counts, confirming that the cross-city EGI pattern was not driven by a few high-posting cities (Supplementary Fig. 23). Local sensitivity of LightGBM outputs was assessed using the finite difference method, which approximated partial derivatives after perturbing each feature by one standard deviation. The numerical partial derivatives were calculated as follows:$${S}_{i,p}=\frac{f\left({x}_{i,p}+{\sigma }_{p}\right)-f\left({x}_{i,p}\right)}{{\sigma }_{p}}$$
                    (12)
                where f denotes the trained LightGBM model, \({x}_{i,p}\) signifies the raw value of the pth feature for the ith sample, and σp corresponds to the standard deviation of that feature. By introducing minor perturbations within the scope of natural variation and monitoring the resultant output shift \(f\left({x}_{i,p}+{\sigma }_{p}\right)-f\left({x}_{i,p}\right)\), the model’s local sensitivity to specific features was quantified, thereby ensuring predictive stability under natural feature fluctuations.LimitationsWe acknowledge certain limitations inherent in this study. Primarily, EGI relied on social media data and was therefore subject to digital demographic bias, potentially overrepresenting younger urban users and underrepresenting elderly and rural groups. This uneven visibility may underestimate expressed emotional perturbations in ageing inland cities, while formal correction requires age-, residence- and platform-participation data unavailable here. Weibo activity was uneven across cities, and posts could not identify whether users were indoors, outdoors, commuting or in air-conditioned environments. Non-climate shocks overlapping with heatwave windows, including local public-health measures, major news events and platform-specific changes in posting behaviour, may also have affected expressed emotions. Although bootstrap and Monte Carlo propagation quantified uncertainty from sentiment measurement and model projection, they could not remove structural uncertainty. The 2010–2024 daily records also limited inference on long-term social adaptation, and future projections assumed stationarity in historical relationships, which may be altered by institutional or adaptation-policy changes. Lexicon-based prescreening and BERT sentiment inference may still miss implicit or context-dependent expressions. Future work should integrate multiplatform social sensing, household surveys, indoor thermal monitoring, mobility data, finer-scale socioeconomic information and large language model-based few-shot relevance screening. Cross-validation with city-level mental health surveillance data from China’s National Mental Health Promotion Action (2021–2030) and longitudinal surveys such as China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) and Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS) should also be prioritized.

Climatic regions comprise tropical–subtropical (TSC), warm temperate (WTC), cold temperate (CTC) and plateau climate (PC), while settlement types comprise megacity cores, small- and medium-sized cities (SME city), other urban areas and rural areas. Centre lines indicate medians, boxes extend from the 25th to the 75th percentiles, whiskers extend to the smallest and largest values within 1.5 times the interquartile range, and values beyond the whiskers are plotted individually as outliers. The lowest and highest plotted observations represent the minima and maxima, respectively. Marginal histograms display univariate distributions.Extended Data Fig. 5 Performance evaluation of the LightGBM model across 19 city clusters.Each panel compares observed values with cross-validated predictions for one city cluster. Dashed diagonal lines indicate perfect agreement. Point colour represents relative sample density, scaled from 0 to 100. Insets report the number of observation–prediction pairs (N), coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute error (MAE) and mean bias (Bias). City-cluster abbreviations are defined in Fig. 1.Extended Data Fig. 6 Taylor diagrams evaluating the performance of 13 CMIP6 global climate models.The diagrams assess model fidelity in simulating daily maximum temperature (Tmax; a, b) and minimum temperature (Tmin; c, d). items.title: A Twist: quando l’upcycling tessile diventa un motore di sostenibilità, creatività e partecipazione

items.body:
La sovrapproduzione è il problema più grande della moda

Upcycling e recycling, perché non sono la stessa cosa

2030: odissea verso il tessile sostenibile e circolare

Nazena, o l’arte del riciclo dei rifiuti tessili
		
		
			La strada per l’economia circolare nel settore tessile è lunga, ma la startup Nazena è nella direzione giusta con la sua tecnica brevettata di riciclo.

Brunello Cucinelli e il principe Carlo insieme per l’Himalaya
		
		
			Brunello Cucinelli finanzierà il prossimo progetto della Fashion task force guidata dal principe Carlo, che aiuterà le comunità indigene dell’Himalaya.

items.title: Clima, agosto 2026 il più caldo della storia
items.description:
Agosto 2026 è stato il mese piu' caldo mai registrato sulla Terra, alla pari con luglio 2023,
The post Clima, agosto 2026 il più caldo della storia ap
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie WWF: “I dati diffusi da Copernicus dovrebbero mobilitare i governi del Pianeta” Agosto mai così caldo da quando si misurano le temperature medie terrestri. Dopo nove mesi, la temperatura globale sale oltre la soglia di 1,5 gradi rispetto all’epoca preindustriale. La temperatura media globale dell’aria superficiale ha raggiunto 16,96 gradi centigradi, 0,85 gradi sopra la media 1991-2020 e 1,65 gradi sopra quella stimata per il periodo preindustriale 1850-1900. A rilevarlo è il Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), implementato dal Centro europeo per le previsioni meteorologiche a medio termine (ECMWF), nel nuovo bollettino climatico mensile. Agosto 2026 è stato il primo mese a superare nuovamente la temperatura media globale di 1,5 gradi centigradi dal novembre 2025. In Europa, gran parte delle regioni occidentali e meridionali hanno registrato temperature sopra la media, con un +3°C di Francia e Italia.  Il dato non riguarda soltanto l’atmosfera. Nell’agosto 2026 la temperatura superficiale media degli oceani, tra 60 gradi Sud e 60 gradi Nord, ha superato i 21°C: è il valore più alto mai osservato per agosto e gli scienziati rilevano che le temperature record per mari e oceani si sono protratte per oltre tre mesi. La crisi climatica sta portando il Pianeta e suoi abitanti verso territori nuovi e potenzialmente molto pericolosi. Già oggi sta producendo fenomeni estremi nell’atmosfera e negli oceani, con impatti sempre più evidenti nelle comunità, nelle economie e negli ecosistemi di tutto il mondo. Questi dati dovrebbero spingere i Governi di tutto il mondo ad agire insieme e in fretta, dovrebbe indurre tutti a mettere la crisi climatica in cima alle priorità. WWF Italia In Europa caldo e siccità, allarme fiumi in secca In Europa il caldo è stato accompagnato da una siccità molto estesa, dalla Gran Bretagna all’Europa Meridionale . Ad agosto condizioni più secche della media hanno interessato alcune aree dell’Europa occidentale e vaste regioni dell’Europa centrale e orientale. I suoli superficiali hanno raggiunto livelli di umidità eccezionalmente bassi nelle zone colpite dalla siccità, mentre aridità e incendi hanno interessato diverse regioni del continente. Particolarmente significativo il segnale proveniente dai maggiori fiumi europei: Danubio e Reno hanno registrato portate eccezionalmente basse. come anche Vistola, Rodano, Senna. In Italia Po e Sesia sono ai minimi storici. Il questionario “Senti già la crisi climatica?” Il WWF Italia invita i cittadini a far emergere il peso dell’impatto dei fenomeni climatici sulla propria vita. Per aiutarli, l’associazione ha promosso, con il sostegno del Movimento Laudato Si’ e altre realtà civiche, un’indagine partecipata per analizzare l’impatto concreto della crisi climatica sulla vita quotidiana della popolazione. Senti già la crisi climatica? Partecipa alla nostra indagine per analizzare l'impatto concreto della crisi climatica nella vita delle persone Partecipa 5 Giugno 2026 Giornata mondiale dell'ambiente, parte l'inchiesta WWF Il WWF lancia un questionario per capire come la crisi climatica sta trasformando la nostra quotidianità 10 Luglio 2026 Clima, un giugno da record L'ondata di calore ha superato i record mensili e storici in vari Paesi europei, provocando gravi ripercussioni sulla salute 1 Luglio 2026 7 italiani su 10 sostengono il principio "chi inquina paga" Nuovo sondaggio europeo: la maggioranza degli intervistati non approverebbe un ridimensionamento del sistema europeo per limitare le emissioni di CO2 nei settori industriali

items.title: La salute di città e cittadini si misura dal ronzio delle api
items.description:
Il nuovo report “La città degli impollinatori” per la decima edizione di Urban Nature: il 3 e 4 ottobre appuntamento nelle piazze italiane 
The post L
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie Il nuovo report in occasione della decima edizione di Urban Nature Gli ambienti urbani che offrono condizioni favorevoli agli impollinatori sono anche ambienti più sani, vivibili e resilienti per le persone. È questo il messaggio al centro del report “La città degli impollinatori: più spazio alla natura, più benessere per le persone”realizzato dal WWF in occasione della decima edizione di Urban Nature 2026: il Festival della natura in città, che si svolgerà in oltre 100 piazze italiane nel weekend del 3 e 4 ottobre. Immagine generata con AI La biodiversità in città Le città ospitano una biodiversità spesso sorprendentemente ricca, costituita da numerose specie vegetali e animali, tra cui gli impollinatori, organismi fondamentali per il funzionamento degli ecosistemi e per la produzione di molti degli alimenti da cui dipendiamo. La presenza di comunità abbondanti e diversificate di impollinatori è generalmente associata ad ambienti urbani ricchi di vegetazione, con una maggiore disponibilità e qualità di habitat, minori livelli di inquinamento e una più elevata capacità di adattarsi agli effetti della crisi climatica. Le stesse caratteristiche che favoriscono gli impollinatori in città – presenza di alberi, prati e fiori, suoli permeabili e una migliore qualità ambientale – contribuiscono anche a migliorare il benessere e la salute delle persone. Alla realizzazione del report ha contribuito anche ISDE –Associazione Medici per l’Ambiente – che parteciperà all’evento del 3 e 4 ottobre di Urban Nature nelle piazze italiane. Oltre i 3/4 delle principali colture alimentari mondiali dipendono dall’impollinazione Oltre il 75% delle principali colture alimentari mondiali dipendono, in misura parziale o totale, dall’impollinazione animale, un servizio ecosistemico essenziale che garantisce la produzione e la qualità di molti degli alimenti che arrivano ogni giorno sulle nostre tavole. Eppure, questi preziosi alleati stanno vivendo un declino senza precedenti: a livello europeo, infatti, quasi il 40% dei sirfidi, il 15% delle farfalle e il 10% delle api selvatiche registrano popolazioni in costante contrazione. Le principali cause del loro declino sono collegabili alla perdita e frammentazione degli habitat, l’intensificazione agricola, l’uso di pesticidi, l’inquinamento e dagli effetti della crisi climatica. Il modello della “Città degli impollinatori” Di fronte a questa emergenza, il WWF propone il modello della “Città degli impollinatori”: una visione che considera gli spazi urbani come parte di una vera e propria rete ecologica. Parchi, prati fioriti, alberature, orti urbani, balconi e tetti verdi sono habitat preziosi sia per gli impollinatori sia per contribuire a rendere le città più fresche, resilienti, meno inquinate e più vivibili per le persone. Il report "La città degli impollinatori" Più spazio alla natura, più benessere alle persone Scopri Il report sottolinea come ogni scelta, pubblica e privata, conti e possa avere un effetto moltiplicatore: la riduzione dell’uso dei pesticidi, la scelta di specie vegetali autoctone e diversificate, la presenza di fioriture distribuite lungo l’anno, il mantenimento di aree naturali e seminaturali e la creazione di piccoli habitat diffusi sono interventi che, se integrati tra loro, possono rafforzare la biodiversità urbana e migliorare la qualità degli ambienti per i cittadini. Immagine generata con AI Gli spazi natura WWF Di fronte alle opportunità che si presentano per migliorare la qualità di vita e il  benessere delle persone con la tutela e l’incremento della natura in città, il WWF risponde da anni con gli Spazi Natura WWF, un fondo che si pone un unico obiettivo, quello di riportare la natura al centro della vita delle persone, creando nuove gemme di biodiversità nei luoghi in cui oggi sono più necessarie: scuole, strutture sanitarie, spazi pubblici e privati, strutture ricettive, aziende, istituti penitenziari e altri contesti urbani ad alta fragilità ambientale e sociale. Grazie ad iniziative come le Oasi urbane, le Aule Natura, le Oasi in Ospedale il WWF si impegna a far tornare il verde nelle nostre vite, rafforzando la biodiversità urbana a favore delle persone, in particolare delle categorie più fragili. Per Urban Nature 2026, “il miele si fa cura” Presso gli stand di Urban Nature i volontari distribuiranno i vasetti di miele “Il miele si fa cura” prodotto da apicoltori impegnati nella conservazione della biodiversità e nella protezione degli impollinatori selvatici. Il messaggio di Urban Nature si inserisce anche nel percorso di attuazione della Nature Restoration Law che, all’articolo 8, stabilisce obiettivi specifici per il ripristino degli ecosistemi urbani, riconoscendo il ruolo del verde e della natura in città anche nelle strategie di adattamento alla crisi climatica. Aumentare e migliorare il verde urbano, la copertura arborea e gli habitat naturali può contribuire a ridurre l’effetto “isola di calore”, migliorare la qualità dell’aria, ridurre il consumo e l’impermeabilizzazione di suolo, tutelare gli impollinatori e rendere le città più sicure, sane e resilienti secondo l’approccio One Health, che riconosce l’interdipendenza tra salute umana, animale e degli ecosistemi. Il Regolamento stabilisce una tabella di marcia chiara – nessuna perdita netta di verde urbano e di copertura arborea entro il 2030 rispetto ai livelli del 2024, e un incremento progressivo a partire dal 2031 – e il WWF chiede a Ministero dell’Ambiente, Regioni e Comuni di attuarla senza ritardi, mettendo a disposizione degli enti locali dati aggiornati e risorse adeguate. Con Urban Nature, il WWF sarà presente in oltre 100 città italiane con stand informativi dove sarà possibile incontrare volontarie e volontari del WWF e scoprire il valore degli Spazi Natura WWF. Sarà inoltre possibile partecipare alle iniziative locali, organizzate dalla rete di volontari WWF e dalle Associazioni Amiche di Urban Nature: ANMS, ISDE, ISPRA, AIIG, APID, ACP, AIGAE, Orti Botanici e altre associazioni locali. Tra gli appuntamenti in programma, anche gli aperitivi scientifici organizzati da WWF Young nella serata di venerdì 2 ottobre.Ragazzi e famiglie potranno inoltre scoprire il valore della Natura in città prendendo parte ad attività outdoor, laboratori didattici, passeggiate naturalistiche, eventi nei musei scientifici e tante altre iniziative. L’evento è patrocinato dal Ministero dell’Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica, ISPRA e da ANMS.   Urban nature 2026 Sabato 3 e Domenica 4 ottobre saremo presenti in più di 100 piazze italiane con i nostri stand  per raccontare il valore della Natura in città ai cittadini, attraverso la distribuzione del miele WWF, che aiuterà a creare il Fondo Spazi Natura WWF.  Vivi la tua città… Scopri di più

items.description: Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta Proponiamo il primo di una serie di post dedicata ad uno degli imp
items.body:
Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta                
												
																																	                
					Ago 31, 2026Ago 31, 20262 commenti su Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta

Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta

Proponiamo il primo di una serie di post dedicata ad uno degli impatti più immediati e devastanti del riscaldamento climatico: gli incendi. Cominciamo col presentare un evento estremo, uno dei due incendi principali che hanno interessato Los Angeles nel gennaio 2025. Innescato nei pressi di un traliccio dell’alta tensione sulle montagne nei pressi di Eaton Canyon, quest’incendio ha devastato un vastissimo versante montuoso e la cittadina di Altadena, distruggendo in poche ore circa 10,000 strutture abitative e commerciali. Un incendio questo verificatosi in seguito alla successione di una siccità di otto mesi ed un intenso evento ventoso di Santa Ana cominciato il 7 gennaio 2025. Un caso più unico che raro o una concreta possibilità anche altrove, oggi o in futuro?

Figura 1: Le fiamme dell’incendio innescato nei pressi di Eaton Canyon avvolgono alcune abitazioni di Altadena in California l’8 gennaio 2025.

Nella notte dell’8 gennaio 2025, i 43,000 abitanti di Altadena, una cittadina a ridosso delle montagne a est di Los Angeles in California, si trovarono a prendere nel giro di qualche minuto una delle decisioni più importante della loro vita.

Durante l’anno precedente (2024), quest’area della California del Sud era stata interessata da un inverno piuttosto piovoso a cui era seguita una siccità pressoché continua durante il resto dell’anno. La successione di un periodo più piovoso del solito ed uno molto arido aveva sviluppato sui ripidi pendii montuosi sovrastanti Altadena una rigogliosa vegetazione arbustiva che, risecchitasi poi durante un periodo siccitoso di 8 mesi, era andata a costituire un significativo accumulo di biomassa potenzialmente combustibile.

La mattina del 7 gennaio 2025 un evento ventoso, riconducibile ai tipici venti di Santa Ana (venti secchi di ricaduta provenienti dalle zone desertiche continentali), cominciò ad interessare le montagne a ridosso di Altadena in maniera molto intensa. Le raffiche di vento arrivarono ad una velocità di 130-160 km/h paragonabili, per dare un’idea, alla forza della tempesta Vaia che nell’autunno del 2018 devastò parte dei boschi delle Alpi Orientali Italiane.

La sera del 7 gennaio 2025 le fiamme si svilupparono dapprima tra i secchi arbusti di macchia mediterranea nei pressi di Eaton Canyon, appena sopra Altadena. Il luogo d’innesco stava proprio al di sotto di un traliccio dell’alta tensione, come riscontrato da videocamere puntate in quella direzione da valle. Un video mostra infatti come quella sera si siano formati degli archi elettrici su un traliccio, probabilmente a causa delle forti raffiche di vento, con conseguente ricaduta di scintille sul terreno sottostante.

Figura 2: Immagine satellitare della cittadina di Altadena quasi completamente avvolta dalle fiamme l’8 gennaio 2025.

A quel punto il fuoco, alimentato dalla diffusa presenza di arbusti secchi e dalle forti raffiche di vento, divenne inarrestabile. Senza che i mezzi aerei antincendio potessero intervenire a causa della tempesta di vento e senza che le squadre di pompieri potessero fronteggiare direttamente le molteplici fiamme a causa del loro vasta diffusione e del calore intensissimo, l’incendio si propagò in poche ore su gran parte del versante montuoso. Dapprima il fuoco procedette da nord verso sud, per poi invertire direzione durante la notte e propagarsi anche tra le abitazioni di Altadena (Fig. 2), in seguito ad una “pioggia” di braci incandescenti trasportate dal vento che agirono da molteplice innesco (spotting) tra le dense abitazioni in legno ed i giardini ricchi di vegetazione ornamentale della cittadina. Uno studio recente relativo agli incendi di Los Angeles ha mostrato come la densità delle strutture sia stato un fattore critico nel causare la distruzione degli edifici durante l’incendio, forse ancora più importante della copertura arborea urbana di cui era ricca Altadena.

Nella notte dell’8 gennaio gli abitanti di Altadena ricevettero un SMS da parte delle autorità che diedero in questo modo l’ordine di evacuazione immediato. La quasi totalità della popolazione abbandonò in pochi minuti le proprie abitazioni, salvando la propria vita ma lasciando al loro destino le abitazioni rimaste senza un presidio che potesse contrastare anche solo molteplici piccoli inneschi causati delle braci trasportate dal vento. In molti casi, una volta penetrato all’interno degli edifici, il fuoco poté svilupparsi rapidamente, fino anche all’accensione quasi simultanea dei materiali combustibili interni (flashover). Da quel momento le case in fiamme diventarono a loro volta sorgenti di calore molto intenso e, generando nuove braci, propagarono il fuoco alle case circostanti. In questo modo circa 10,000 strutture abitative e commerciali di Altadena vennero completamente distrutte (Fig. 3).

Figura 3: La cittadina di Altadena quasi completamente devastata nei giorni immediatamente successivi all’incendio.

L’8 gennaio 2025 le vittime ad Altadena furono 19, una perdita drammatica ma un numero relativamente ridotto per un evento di tali dimensioni, grazie soprattutto alla rapida ed efficiente esecuzione della procedura di evacuazione della popolazione. Dopo aver distrutto gran parte degli edifici di Altadena, nei giorni successivi l’incendio si propagò sui versanti montuosi sovrastanti per 25 km fino a 2000 metri di quota interessando un’area totale di 5674 ettari prima di essere contenuto dai mezzi aerei antincendio entrati finalmente in azione dopo la cessazione delle intense raffiche di vento di Santa Ana.

Quella notte dell’8 gennaio in pochi minuti la comunità di Altadena si era stata salvata ma allo stesso tempo era anche stata sradicata dal suo territorio, senza una concreta possibilità di ritorno a breve termine e, in molti casi, anche a lungo termine. In seguito, il 5% degli abitanti hanno deciso infatti di vendere quello che restava delle loro proprietà, una volta bonificate dalle macerie e dalle ceneri delle case distrutte dall’incendio. L’incendio, distruggendo le abitazioni e strutture, aveva di fatto reso disponibili nuovi terreni edificabili per il mercato e la speculazione edilizia.

Per comprendere questa conseguenza, forse inaspettata, è necessario considerare il contesto attuale dell’edilizia abitativa in California: in breve mancano case e quindi la domanda è di gran lunga superiore all’offerta. Le cause di questo fenomeno sono ben spiegate nel libro di Francesco Costa, “California fine del sogno” ma sostanzialmente alcune leggi californiane di protezione ambientale sono state usate per impedire la costruzione di nuove case popolari per non diminuire il valore delle singole abitazioni adiacenti. L’incendio del Gennaio 2025 ha scombinato questa situazione di stallo ad Altadena ed ha dato il via libera alla costruzione di nuove case, più moderne e probabilmente con più appartamenti. Oggi un lotto di terreno completamente bruciato vale una cifra dell’ordine di mezzo milione di dollari ad Altadena mentre due terzi dei lotti effettivamente venduti sono stati acquistati da investitori. Tuttavia, la ricostruzione non sta procedendo velocemente: un rapporto indica che nove mesi dopo l’incendio 7 abitazioni gravemente danneggiate su 10 non mostravano ancora alcun segno di progresso verso la ricostruzione, in particolare le case di proprietari afroamericani e asiatici, maggiormente esposti a problemi di accesso alle risorse necessarie e al fenomeno della sottoassicurazione.

Impossibile quantificare precisamente l’enorme danno economico e morale sofferto da Altadena e dai suoi abitanti. Tuttavia il fondo californiano di assicurazione per gli incendi ha pagato fino ad ora 22367 richieste di risarcimento (su un totale di 22890) per danni a proprietà residenziali ($ 7.39 miliardi , inclusi i danni anche per solo inquinamento da fumi); 1079 (su 1262) a proprietà commerciali ($ 532 milioni) e 3392 (su 3814) a auto private e commerciali ($ 62 milioni). Un bilancio grave per le assicurazioni che tuttavia non avranno probabilmente particolari problemi ad assicurare le nuove abitazioni che verranno realizzate con materiali ignifughi e saranno protette da sistemi e procedure antincendio adeguate. L’8 gennaio del 2025 Altadena è bruciata anche perché dal cielo pioveva letteralmente fuoco su vecchie case di legno.

Di fronte a tale devastazione viene da chiedersi: ma l’incendio che ha distrutto gran parte di Altadena è risultato in seguito ad una successione di eventi (una lunga siccità e l’intenso evento ventoso di Santa Ana) che sono possibili solo nella California del Sud? E questo incendio è stato il risultato prevedibile di eventi che si erano già presentati nel passato? E non ultimo, i cambiamenti climatici in corso hanno avuto un ruolo nel determinare i fattori scatenanti l’incendio, ovvero la lunghissima siccità e l’intenso evento ventoso di Santa Ana?  Cercare di rispondere a queste domande è importante per cominciare a capire se eventi come questo siano potenzialmente riproducibili in altre zone del pianeta oggi oppure in futuro.  Questo è l’argomento che tratteremo nel prossimo post dedicato agli incendi.

Testo di Paolo Gabrielli con contributi di Giorgio Vacchiano, Mario Grosso e Luigi Pasotti
